lead: A V-n diagram is a graph of load factor n against airspeed V for one aircraft. It shows the largest n the wing can produce before it stalls at each speed, and the largest n the structure is allowed to carry. Its corners are the critical cases used to size the wing, fuselage and tail.
prereq: You need limit load and load factor from Loads on aircraft and design considerations.

blocks.text: Load factor n is lift divided by weight, n = L/W. At a given speed V the wing can make lift only up to its stall limit. Let C<sub>Lmax</sub> be the maximum lift coefficient in the configuration used for the diagram. The one-g stall speed V<sub>S1</sub> is the speed at which level flight needs the whole C<sub>Lmax</sub>. From L = ½ ρ V² S C<sub>L</sub>, with L = W at n = 1:

blocks.where: W/S is wing loading in N/m²; ρ is air density in kg/m³; C<sub>Lmax</sub> is dimensionless.

blocks.text: At a higher speed the same wing can pull more load factor before it stalls. Put L = nW in the lift equation and divide by the one-g case. The ρ, S and C<sub>Lmax</sub> cancel:

blocks.where: n is load factor (dimensionless); V is true airspeed in m/s; V<sub>S1</sub> is the one-g stall speed in m/s.

blocks.text: This is the stall line. It is a parabola, not a straight line. At V = V<sub>S1</sub> it gives n = 1; at 2V<sub>S1</sub> it gives n = 4. The wing cannot go above this line at that speed, because it stalls.

sections.h3: Limit load factors, V<sub>A</sub>, V<sub>C</sub>, V<sub>D</sub> and gusts

blocks.text: The structure has a positive limit load factor n<sub>max</sub> and a negative limit n<sub>min</sub>: for transport aircraft at least 2.5 and −1.0, for light aircraft about 3.8 and −1.5. These are limit values. The positive stall line meets n<sub>max</sub> at the manoeuvre speed V<sub>A</sub>:

blocks.where: V<sub>A</sub> is the manoeuvre speed in m/s; V<sub>S1</sub> is the one-g stall speed in m/s; n<sub>max</sub> is the positive limit load factor.

blocks.text: From V<sub>A</sub> the top stays flat at n<sub>max</sub> all the way to V<sub>D</sub>, the design dive speed; V<sub>C</sub>, the design cruising speed, lies between them. The bottom is not a mirror image: the negative stall line uses the smaller negative lift coefficient, n = −(V/V<sub>S,neg</sub>)², and for transport aircraft n<sub>min</sub> stays at −1.0 up to V<sub>C</sub>, then rises in a straight line to 0 at V<sub>D</sub>. A vertical line at V<sub>D</sub> closes the envelope.
A sharp vertical gust of speed U changes the angle of attack by U/V, and the lift-curve slope a (per radian) turns this into extra lift:
n = 1 ± ρ V a U / (2 W/S)
blocks.where: ρ is air density in kg/m³; V is airspeed in m/s; a is the lift-curve slope per radian; U is the gust velocity in m/s; W/S is the wing loading in N/m². Use + for an upward gust and − for a downward one.

blocks.text: Each gust line is straight and starts at n = 1 when V = 0. Textbook design gusts (equivalent airspeed) are about 20 m/s at V<sub>B</sub>, 15 m/s at V<sub>C</sub> and 7.5 m/s at V<sub>D</sub>. This is the sharp-edged value; certification multiplies the increment by a gust alleviation factor below 1. At low speed the gust line lies above the stall line, where the wing stalls first; at V<sub>C</sub> it can end above n<sub>max</sub>, a gust load larger than any manoeuvre the pilot may command.

sections.h3: Reading the critical corners: wing, fuselage and tail

blocks.text: The critical points are the corners A (V<sub>A</sub>, n<sub>max</sub>) and D (V<sub>D</sub>, n<sub>max</sub>), the negative corners at V<sub>C</sub> and V<sub>D</sub>, and any gust point outside the manoeuvre boundary. Each gives a load factor and the speed at which it acts.

items: Wing: root bending grows with n, so the highest corner sizes the spar caps and skins. Torsion depends on speed as well, because the wing’s nose-down pitching moment grows with dynamic pressure, so the V<sub>D</sub> corners usually size the torsion box.

Fuselage: the corner n is the inertia factor on every mass in the fuselage; each seat, galley, cargo item and rear-mounted engine pushes down with n m g. With the tail load at that corner, it sets the fuselage bending moment.

Tail unit: the tailplane load at each corner comes from pitching-moment balance, worked in Stress analysis of fuselage and tail unit. The largest balancing loads usually appear at VA, with the largest n, and at VD, with the largest wing pitching moment. Checked pitching manoeuvres and full-elevator cases at VA are added. The fin is sized by rudder and sideslip cases from VA to VD, which the V-n diagram does not show.

figure.caption: The V-n diagram of the worked examples: stall line to A (90.4 m/s, 2.5), flat top to D at 160 m/s, negative limit −1.0 to F at 120 m/s and 0 at E. The 15 m/s gust line ends at n = 2.84 at V<sub>C</sub>, above the manoeuvre top, so it sizes upward bending.

spec.aria: V-n diagram with speed from 0 to 180 metres per second and load factor from minus 1.5 to 3.2. A parabolic stall line rises from the origin through 1.0 at 57.1 metres per second to corner A at 90.4 and 2.5; the flat top runs to D at 160; the envelope closes at E. The negative side follows a stall curve to minus 1.0, stays flat to F at 120, then rises to zero at 160. Dashed gust lines from n equal 1 at zero speed reach 2.84 and minus 0.84 at 120, and 2.23 and minus 0.23 at 160.

examples.question: A wing has wing loading W/S = 3000 N/m² and C<sub>Lmax</sub> = 1.5. Air density is 1.225 kg/m³. The positive limit load factor is n<sub>max</sub> = 2.5. Find the one-g stall speed V<sub>S1</sub> and the manoeuvre speed V<sub>A</sub>. State where the first manoeuvre corner lies.
steps: At n = 1: W/S = ½ ρ V<sub>S1</sub>² C<sub>Lmax</sub>. Rearrange: V<sub>S1</sub> = √(2(W/S)/(ρ C<sub>Lmax</sub>)).

Below 90.4 m/s the wing stalls before it reaches n = 2.5; above it the wing can reach 2.5. So the first manoeuvre corner is (V<sub>A</sub>, n<sub>max</sub>) = (90.4 m/s, 2.5), and the flat top runs from there to V<sub>D</sub>.
examples.answer: V<sub>S1</sub> = 57.1 m/s and V<sub>A</sub> = 90.4 m/s; the manoeuvre corner is at (90.4 m/s, 2.5).
examples.check:
W<sub>S</sub> = 3000.0
rho = 1.225
CLmax = 1.5
n<sub>max</sub> = 2.5
VS1 = (2 * W<sub>S</sub> / (rho * CLmax)) ** 0.5
VA = VS1 * (n<sub>max</sub> ** 0.5)
print(round(VS1, 1))
print(round(VA, 1))

examples.question: The same aircraft (W/S = 3000 N/m², ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, n<sub>max</sub> = 2.5, n<sub>min</sub> = −1.0) has V<sub>C</sub> = 120 m/s and V<sub>D</sub> = 160 m/s. The lift-curve slope is a = 5.0 per radian. Using sharp-edged gusts of 15 m/s at V<sub>C</sub> and 7.5 m/s at V<sub>D</sub>, find the gust load factors and say whether a gust or the manoeuvre limit sizes the wing for upward bending.
steps: Only 2.84 lies outside the manoeuvre limits (2.5 and −1.0).
The upward gust at V<sub>C</sub> is critical: 2.84 ÷ 2.5 = 1.135, so the wing root bending is about 13.5 % higher than for the manoeuvre corner.
examples.answer: Gust load factors are 2.84 and −0.84 at V<sub>C</sub>, 2.23 and −0.23 at V<sub>D</sub>. The upward gust at V<sub>C</sub> (n = 2.84) sizes the wing for upward bending, not the manoeuvre limit of 2.5.

traps: Drawing the stall line as a straight line from the origin to V<sub>A</sub>. It is n = (V/V<sub>S1</sub>)², a parabola; a straight line under-predicts n at mid speeds.

Mirroring the top of the envelope to make the bottom. The negative stall line uses the smaller negative lift coefficient, and n<sub>min</sub> rises from −1.0 at V<sub>C</sub> to 0 at V<sub>D</sub> for transport aircraft.
Ending the flat top at V<sub>C</sub>. For transport aircraft the positive limit n<sub>max</sub> holds all the way to V<sub>D</sub>.
Ignoring gust lines at high speed. A gust point at V<sub>C</sub> can sit above the manoeuvre top, so the critical load may be a gust the pilot never commands.
Rounding V<sub>S1</sub> too early. 57.14 × √2.5 = 90.35 m/s; using 57.1 gives 90.3 m/s. Keep full precision until the final answer.

quiz.q: Define the one-g stall speed V<sub>S1</sub>.
quiz.a: V<sub>S1</sub> is the lowest speed at which the wing can carry the aircraft weight in level flight at n = 1 with the selected C<sub>Lmax</sub>.

quiz.q: Why is the negative half of a transport aircraft’s V-n diagram smaller than the positive half?
quiz.a: The negative lift coefficient the wing can reach is smaller than the positive one, so the negative stall line rises more slowly, and the rules set n<sub>min</sub> at only −1.0 (against +2.5), rising to 0 at V<sub>D</sub>. Pushovers and downward gusts load the structure less than pull-ups.

quiz.q: W/S = 3000 N/m², ρ = 1.225 kg/m³ and a = 5.0 per radian. Find the upward gust load factor for a 10 m/s gust at 100 m/s.
A gust line ends above n<sub>max</sub> at V<sub>C</sub>. What does this mean for wing, fuselage and tail sizing?
quiz.a: The aircraft can meet a load factor larger than the manoeuvre limit in a gust, so the gust point, not the stall corner, sets the largest bending load on the wing. The same n multiplies every fuselage mass, so the fuselage bending case is also taken at that gust point, with the tail load needed to balance it.

quiz.q: Why is full control deflection at V<sub>D</sub> dangerous even below n<sub>max</sub>?
quiz.a: The V-n diagram limits the aircraft load factor, not local loads. At V<sub>D</sub> the dynamic pressure is highest, so full deflection gives large hinge moments, tail loads and wing torsion; these cases are checked separately and can be critical below n<sub>max</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the V-n diagram summarises thousands of load cases from a digital loads model. Certification adds discrete gust and continuous turbulence cases, and flexible wings are checked for aeroelastic effects on the gust response. Search for gust load factor, manoeuvre envelope and CS-25 load cases.
